newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Budget pact deal lifts shadow from EU summit.
newsitem.headline: Budget pact deal lifts shadow from EU summit.

text.p: European Union finance ministers clinched agreement on Monday on a pact that will link budget discipline among members of the bloc's planned single currency to economic growth and jobs.

The accord lifted one of the main obstacles to progress at a two-day summit of EU leaders, defusing what had threatened to be a serious rift between Bonn and Paris, the bloc's twin economic and political powerhouses.
"We have reached complete agreement on the stability pact and the resolution for growth and employment," Dutch Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm told reporters.

The finance ministers were meeting in the wings of the summit which was expected to agree a new treaty paving the way for enlargement and winning back voters' confidence through measures to promote a free, safe and just Citizens' Europe.
But those negotiations had been largely sidetracked by the Franco-German split over how to cement monetary union, due to be launched in January 1999.
Zalm declined to detail the agreement, which finance ministers were due to report to their leaders later on Monday.

But EU monetary affairs commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said the accord provided for a special lending programme by the European Investment Bank (EIB) to help small businesses and high-technology companies.
The EU leaders were expected later to sanction a special "jobs summit" in the autumn.
The link goes some way to meeting demands by the new French Socialist government that Europe should pay more attention to the bloc's 18 million jobless.

A spokeswoman for French President Jacques Chirac said that both he and his left-wing Prime Minister Lionel Jospin welcomed the accord, "obtained thanks to a perfect coordination between the President and the Prime Minister".
"This is only a beginning. We have begun to reverse the trend. We have loosened the noose," a spokesman for Jospin told reporters.
Professing his satisfaction, German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said the stability pact was on "a good path."

Dutch Secretary of State for European Affairs Michiel Patijn earlier signalled a brisk start to the long-running inter-governmental conference (IGC) treaty review, saying that an employment chapter had largely been agreed, providing for limited EU-backed incentives and pilot projects and annual guidelines on measures to promote job-creation.

"(It) strikes a fair balance between efficient cooperation and the realisation that principle responsibility for employment rests with member states," an aide quoted British Prime Minister Tony Blair as saying.
Chirac earlier appealed to his EU partners to try to give Europe a more social face and do more for the bloc's unemployed.

"We must reconcile European citizens with Europe. That means setting clear priorities. It also means giving the Union more effective ways of supporting member states' efforts and ensuring the preservation and reinforcement of the Euorpean social model," Chirac said, according to a text of his remarks.
Leaders were to continue working through a draft treaty on Monday before ordering a new version to be written overnight for agreement on Tuesday.
The treaty, the result of more than 15 months' negotiation, is expected to offer the bloc's citizens a broad range of freedoms and lift internal borders across the continent.

But it is likely to cover up sharp differences between the fervent integrationists who want to move ahead of others if they wish and others who seek opt-outs and protocols to protect vital national positions.
A tough fight was also expected over plans to reform EU institutions before planned enlargement into eastern Europe in the next decade.
